templates.name: Present or describe to an already familiar audience
Introduce or describe to an unfamiliar or new audience
Explain (cause, origin, advantage, mechanism, definition, significance)
Specify or identify a single fact

items.subtype: Explain why (mechanism over a chain of bullets)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Flat stones are occasionally found balanced on thin ice columns on Siberia’s frozen Lake Baikal.
• Known as Baikal zen stones, these formations appear where strong winds have swept away the snow.
• In the exceptionally dry winter air, exposed ice sublimates, transforming into vapor without melting.
• A stone shields the ice below it from the sun, so that ice sublimates more slowly than the surrounding ice.
• Similar formations on mountain glaciers, called glacier tables, develop in summer as surrounding ice melts.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why Baikal zen stones end up balanced atop columns of ice. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Like glacier tables, Baikal zen stones end up on columns because in summer the ice around each stone melts in the sunlight while the ice beneath the stone remains frozen.
Found where strong winds have swept away the snow on Lake Baikal, zen stones are flat stones balanced on thin ice columns.
Because each stone shields the ice beneath it from sunlight, that ice turns to vapor more slowly than the exposed ice around it, leaving the stone raised.
In the exceptionally dry winter air over Lake Baikal, exposed ice sublimates, turning directly into vapor rather than melting.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain why the stones end up on columns of ice. The notes say that “exposed ice sublimates” in the dry winter air and that a stone “shields the ice below it from the sun, so that ice sublimates more slowly than the surrounding ice.” Choice C links the two facts: the exposed ice wears away faster, so the shaded ice is left as a column under the stone.

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: glacier process applied to Baikal)
A.why_wrong: It explains the columns, but with the process the notes give for glacier tables. The notes say Baikal’s exposed ice sublimates in winter, “transforming into vapor without melting,” not that it melts in summer.

B.recipe: OG (describes the formations and where they appear)
B.why_wrong: It says what the stones look like and where they are found but does not explain why they end up on columns.

D.why_wrong: It describes the sublimation of exposed ice but never mentions the stones or the shade they cast, so it does not explain why a stone ends up raised.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ice physics). Real phenomenon known without a search (zen stones on Baikal ice; shading slows sublimation under the stone; glacier tables form by differential melting); no researcher named (WAVE.md, no fact-checking for this skill). Band 6: one goal-shaped FALSE (the glacier mechanism transferred to Baikal), one OG, one PART that gives the process without the link to the stone; key paraphrases sublimation as turning to vapor.

band7.why: Targeted band 6. Explain-why over a three-bullet chain; one goal-shaped FALSE (glacier-table summer melting transferred to Baikal), one OG, one PART; key derives the raised stone from shading plus sublimation. Only one FALSE option keeps it below band 7.

review.notes: Baikal also appears in live boundaries w3b2_21 (Baikal seal); different subject.

items.subtype: Present the findings (two numeric findings, key drops the numbers)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Virtual fencing uses GPS collars to keep livestock in place without conventional fences.
• When an animal approaches a boundary, its collar sounds an audio warning, then administers a mild electric pulse.
• In one study, researchers put these collars on cattle and designated an exclusion zone along a stream.
• Finding: The collars kept the cattle outside the designated zone 96% of the time.
• Finding: Over the summer, pulses per animal fell by 70% as the cattle increasingly retreated at the audio warning.
items.stem: The student wants to present the findings of the study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The collars kept the cattle outside the zone nearly all the time, the researchers found, and the animals needed far fewer pulses as they increasingly turned back at the warning.
The researchers found that the collars reduced the cattle’s visits to the exclusion zone by 70% over the summer and that 96% of the animals retreated at the audio warning.
The cattle stayed outside the exclusion zone along the stream 96% of the time, the researchers found, and over the summer each animal needed 70% fewer audio warnings before it retreated.
To test virtual fencing, researchers put GPS collars on cattle and designated an exclusion zone along a stream in their pasture.
items.explanation: The study has two findings: the collars “kept the cattle outside the designated zone 96% of the time,” and “pulses per animal fell by 70% as the cattle increasingly retreated at the audio warning.” Choice A presents both, keeping each result attached to what it measured.

B.why_wrong: The 70% figure describes the drop in pulses, not in visits to the zone, and 96% is the share of time the cattle stayed outside the zone, not the share of animals that retreated at the warning.

C.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: the 70% moved from pulses to audio warnings)
C.why_wrong: The first finding is right, but the 70% drop the notes report is in “pulses per animal,” not in audio warnings; the notes give no figure for warnings at all.

D.why_wrong: It describes how the study was set up, not what the researchers found.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and technology (livestock management). Unnamed, plainly generic study; the figures are invented and attached to no real study or company (WAVE.md wave-3 lesson); no collar brand named. Option fact check: B FALSE goal-shaped (both numbers on the wrong measures), C FALSE goal-shaped (70% moved from pulses to warnings; reviewer replaced a plain reversal, "increasingly frequent pulses", that one glance at the notes killed), D true but off-goal. Goal-only solve (notes hidden): A, B and C all present two findings.
band7_moves: present-the-findings goal over two numeric findings
key drops both numbers and restates them qualitatively
two goal-shaped FALSE options that present both findings: one moves each number onto the wrong measure, one moves the 70% from pulses to audio warnings

band7.why: Present-the-findings goal over two numeric findings, as band-7 official 5645f119; the key drops both numbers; B and C each present two findings and misattach a number (B both, C the 70% moved from pulses to warnings), so a goal-only solve leaves A, B and C; D is an accurate off-goal method; notes 24% rare words. Leans on number checking rather than a derived relation.

fixes: C was an obvious reversal ("increasingly frequent pulses"); now a goal-shaped misattachment of the 70% figure to audio warnings

items.subtype: Overview of a trade route (source, route, exchange)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Over many centuries, camel caravans transported goods across the Sahara between North and West Africa.
• Among the most valuable commodities was salt, which was scarce in the agricultural regions south of the desert.
• At Taghaza, a Saharan mining settlement, workers cut salt into enormous slabs; even buildings were constructed from salt blocks.
• Caravans transported the slabs south to trading centers such as Timbuktu.
• There, merchants exchanged the salt for gold originating in mines farther south in West Africa.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the salt trade described in the notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Salt was so plentiful at Taghaza, a mining settlement in the Sahara, that workers there even constructed buildings from blocks of it.
Gold from West African mines was transported north by camel caravan to Taghaza, where merchants exchanged it for enormous slabs of salt.
Over many centuries, camel caravans transported salt, a commodity scarce in the agricultural regions south of the Sahara, across the desert.
Salt cut into slabs at Taghaza, in the Sahara, was transported by caravan to trading centers such as Timbuktu and exchanged there for West African gold.
items.explanation: An overview should cover the whole trade: where the salt came from, where it went and what it was exchanged for. Choice D traces the salt from Taghaza, where workers “cut salt into enormous slabs,” to “trading centers such as Timbuktu,” where “merchants exchanged the salt for gold originating in mines farther south in West Africa.”

A.why_wrong: It gives a striking detail about the mining settlement but says nothing about where the salt was carried or what it was exchanged for.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: route and place of exchange reversed)
B.why_wrong: It sketches the whole trade but reverses it: the notes say the salt was carried south to Timbuktu and exchanged there, not that gold was carried north to Taghaza.

C.recipe: PART (one component: the caravans and why salt was valuable)
C.why_wrong: It mentions the caravans and why salt was valued but leaves out where the salt came from, where it went and what it was exchanged for.

items.notes: Subject: history (trans-Saharan trade). Well-known facts stated without a search (salt slabs mined at Taghaza, buildings of salt blocks, caravans to Timbuktu, salt exchanged for gold); no dates or figures given. Band 6: one goal-shaped FALSE (reversed route), one OG, one PART; key compresses three bullets.

band7.why: Targeted band 6. Overview with OG, goal-shaped FALSE (trade direction reversed) and PART (transport without the exchange), as band-6 officials 1773fa73 and b44141cf; the key is the only option covering source, route and exchange.

items.subtype: Present the study’s findings to an audience already familiar with the term
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Zombie fires are wildfires that smolder underground throughout winter and flare up in spring.
• They burn in peat, a thick layer of partially decomposed vegetation common in northern forests.
• A team of researchers used satellite imagery to find zombie fires in Alaska and northern Canada.
• The team found that zombie fires were most frequent after hot summers with extensive wildfires.
• Hot summers may dry out peat, allowing fires to penetrate deep enough to survive winter.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s findings to an audience already familiar with zombie fires. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Researchers found that wildfires that smolder underground throughout winter and flare up in spring, known as zombie fires, were most frequent after hot summers.
Analyzing satellite imagery of Alaska and northern Canada, researchers found that zombie fires were most frequent after hot summers with extensive wildfires.
Zombie fires, which burn through the winter in peat, a layer of partially decomposed vegetation, were identified in Alaska and northern Canada by researchers using satellite imagery.
Hot summers may dry out peat enough to let zombie fires burn deep underground, where they can survive until spring.
items.explanation: The audience already knows what zombie fires are, so the sentence should use the term without defining it and give what the team found. Choice B does this: it identifies the study, which “used satellite imagery to find zombie fires in Alaska and northern Canada,” and its finding that the fires “were most frequent after hot summers with extensive wildfires.”

A.why_wrong: It gives the finding but spends much of the sentence explaining what a zombie fire is, which this audience already knows.

C.recipe: AUD and PART (definition plus method, no finding)
C.why_wrong: It explains where zombie fires burn and how the researchers identified them but never says what the team found.

D.recipe: OG (possible explanation offered for the finding)
D.why_wrong: It gives a possible reason that hot summers matter, which the notes hedge with “may,” but it does not present what the team found.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (boreal wildfire). Real phenomenon known without a search (overwintering or zombie fires in boreal peat, more frequent after hot summers with large fires, found with satellite data); the team is unnamed and no figures are given. Band 6 as planned: AUD, AUD plus PART, and an interpretation-for-finding OG.

band7.why: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items. Shape of band-6 official 39ccb463 (AUD, AUD, PART/OG): two options define zombie fires for an audience that knows them, one gives the hypothesis.

items.subtype: Explanation and an example of a term (with a subtype)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Reduplication is a linguistic process that repeats all or part of a word to create a new meaning.
• Full reduplication repeats an entire word, whereas partial reduplication duplicates only a portion.
• In Indonesian, full reduplication can indicate plurality: orang means “person,” and orang-orang means “people.”
• In Tagalog, partial reduplication can indicate future action: bili means “buy,” and bibili means “will buy.”
items.stem: The student wants to provide an explanation and an example of full reduplication. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Reduplication, a linguistic process that repeats all or part of a word to create a new meaning, takes two forms, one of which is called full reduplication.
In full reduplication, only a portion of a word is repeated, as when the Tagalog word bili (“buy”) becomes bibili (“will buy”).
In Indonesian, the word orang means “person,” and the word orang-orang means “people.”
Full reduplication repeats an entire word to create a new meaning; in Indonesian, for instance, orang (“person”) becomes orang-orang (“people”).
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: explain full reduplication and give an example of it. Choice D explains that full reduplication “repeats an entire word” and gives the Indonesian example from the notes, in which orang (“person”) becomes orang-orang (“people”).

A.why_wrong: It explains reduplication in general and names full reduplication but never says what full reduplication does or gives an example of it.

B.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: partial reduplication passed off as full)
B.why_wrong: It describes partial reduplication, not full, and the Tagalog example is one the notes give for partial reduplication.

C.why_wrong: It gives the Indonesian words but never explains what full reduplication is or that these words show it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics). Standard textbook examples stated without a search (Indonesian orang-orang, Tagalog bili and bibili). The plan set band_target 7, but EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so it is written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md: a goal-shaped FALSE (wrong subtype and wrong example), the explanation-only PART and the example-only PART.

band7.why: EXAMPLE has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; written as a strong band 6 like official ec03f090 (PART, FALSE, PART): B is a goal-shaped FALSE pairing the partial-reduplication definition and Tagalog example with "full reduplication".

items.subtype: Contrast two kinds on the attribute the goal names
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glaciologists classify glaciers partly by the temperature at their base.
• A cold-based glacier is frozen solidly to the bedrock beneath it.
• Cold-based glaciers advance mainly through the gradual deformation of their ice and cause minimal erosion.
• A warm-based glacier rests on a thin layer of meltwater above the bedrock.
• Warm-based glaciers slide across this water and can scrape away substantial amounts of rock.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how the two kinds of glaciers move. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Whereas a cold-based glacier advances mainly through the gradual deformation of its ice, a warm-based glacier slides across a thin layer of meltwater.
Cold-based and warm-based glaciers both move, though they don’t do so in exactly the same way.
Warm-based glaciers can scrape away substantial amounts of rock, but cold-based glaciers cause minimal erosion.
Resting on a thin layer of meltwater above the bedrock, a warm-based glacier slides across the water and can scrape away substantial amounts of rock.
items.explanation: The goal asks how the two kinds of glaciers differ in the way they move. Choice A contrasts them: cold-based glaciers “advance mainly through the gradual deformation of their ice,” whereas warm-based glaciers “slide across” a thin layer of meltwater.

B.recipe: VAGUE (says they differ without saying how)
B.why_wrong: It says the glaciers move in different ways but never says what those ways are.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts how much the two kinds of glaciers erode, not how they move.

D.why_wrong: It explains how a warm-based glacier moves but says nothing about cold-based glaciers.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (glaciology). Standard textbook distinction stated without a search; no researcher or place named.

items.subtype: Contrast two regional styles (one shared trait, one difference)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Navajo weavers in different regions developed distinctive rug styles.
• Two Grey Hills rugs, from northwestern New Mexico, are woven entirely from natural, undyed wool.
• Their colors are limited to the natural white, gray, brown, and black of fleece.
• Ganado rugs, from northeastern Arizona, are recognized for their deep red backgrounds.
• This red is typically combined with geometric designs in black, white, and gray.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between Two Grey Hills rugs and Ganado rugs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both Two Grey Hills rugs and Ganado rugs include the colors black, white, and gray.
Navajo weavers in different regions, including northwestern New Mexico and northeastern Arizona, developed distinctive rug styles.
While Two Grey Hills rugs are limited to the natural colors of undyed wool, Ganado rugs are recognized for their deep red backgrounds.
Ganado rugs, which come from northeastern Arizona, are recognized for deep red backgrounds typically combined with geometric designs in black, white, and gray.
items.explanation: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must contrast the two styles on the same feature. Choice C does this with color: Two Grey Hills rugs are limited to “the natural white, gray, brown, and black of fleece,” while Ganado rugs are “recognized for their deep red backgrounds.”

A.why_wrong: It points out colors the two styles share, which emphasizes a similarity rather than a difference.

B.why_wrong: It says the styles come from different regions but does not say how the rugs themselves differ.

D.why_wrong: It describes Ganado rugs but says nothing about Two Grey Hills rugs, so it does not contrast the two.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Navajo weaving). Well-known regional styles stated without a search (Two Grey Hills: natural undyed wool; Ganado: deep red ground with black, white and gray); no weaver named. Distinct from the live TSP subject Melissa Cody (one contemporary weaver).

review.notes: Soft overlap judged acceptable: Navajo weaving also appears in live TSP Melissa Cody (one contemporary Germantown Revival weaver) and official CID dc3ea63e (Lillie Taylor plant dyes); this item is the regional-style contrast (Two Grey Hills vs Ganado), a distinct subject, but it makes a three-item Navajo-weaving cluster.

items.subtype: Contrast two kinds (definition pair)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Foreign aid includes grants and loans that wealthier countries provide to support development.
• Some aid is tied, meaning it must be spent on goods or services from the donor country.
• Untied aid can be spent on goods or services from any country.
• Tied aid can raise the costs of projects, since recipients cannot choose the cheapest supplier.
• In 2001, many donor countries agreed to untie most of their aid to the least developed countries.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between tied aid and untied aid. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because recipients cannot choose the cheapest supplier, tied aid can raise the costs of development projects.
Whereas tied aid must be spent on goods or services from the donor country, untied aid can be spent on those from any country.
Tied aid and untied aid are both forms of foreign aid, but they come with different conditions for the countries that receive them.
In 2001, many donor countries agreed to untie most of the grants and loans they provide to the least developed countries.
items.explanation: The sentence must state how the two kinds of aid differ. Choice B contrasts them on the same point, where the money may be spent: tied aid “must be spent on goods or services from the donor country,” whereas untied aid “can be spent on goods or services from any country.”

A.why_wrong: It describes a drawback of tied aid but says nothing about untied aid.

C.recipe: VAGUE (says they differ without saying how)
C.why_wrong: It says the two kinds of aid come with different conditions but never says what those conditions are.

D.why_wrong: It reports an agreement to untie aid but does not explain how tied and untied aid differ.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of development). Standard definitions stated without a search; the 2001 agreement is the OECD Development Assistance Committee recommendation to untie aid to the least developed countries, left unnamed. Replaces a census item withdrawn as too close to rhetorical_synthesis.DIFF.medium.w2b5_07.

items.subtype: Describe a person’s work to an audience unfamiliar with the person
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ablade Glover is a Ghanaian painter born in 1934.
• He taught art at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Kumasi.
• Glover applies thick layers of paint with a palette knife rather than a brush.
• His paintings frequently depict crowded outdoor markets, with figures rendered as dense patches of vivid color.
• He also founded the Artists Alliance Gallery, an exhibition space in Accra.
items.stem: The student wants to describe Glover’s paintings to an audience unfamiliar with the artist. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Made by applying thick layers of paint with a palette knife, Glover’s paintings frequently depict crowded outdoor markets, with figures rendered as dense patches of vivid color.
Ghanaian painter Ablade Glover, born in 1934, taught art at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Kumasi.
The Artists Alliance Gallery, an exhibition space in Accra, was founded by Ghanaian painter Ablade Glover.
Ghanaian painter Ablade Glover uses a palette knife to apply thick layers of paint, often depicting crowded markets whose figures appear as dense patches of vivid color.
items.explanation: Because the audience does not know Glover, the sentence should say who he is before describing his paintings. Choice D identifies him as a “Ghanaian painter” and then describes how he paints, with “a palette knife,” and what he paints, “crowded outdoor markets, with figures rendered as dense patches of vivid color.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the paintings well but uses Glover’s name without saying who he is, which this audience would need.

B.why_wrong: It introduces Glover but says nothing about his paintings.

C.recipe: OG (the gallery instead of the paintings)
C.why_wrong: It tells who founded a gallery but does not describe Glover’s paintings.

items.notes: Subject: arts (painting). Real artist; facts stated from general knowledge without a search (Ghanaian painter born 1934, taught at KNUST in Kumasi, thick palette-knife paintings of crowds and markets, founder of the Artists Alliance Gallery in Accra); no titled work or other figure given.

fixes: key said the markets were depicted "as dense patches of vivid color"; the notes say the figures are; key and explanation corrected

items.subtype: Introduce a concept to a new audience
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cumulonimbus clouds are towering, dense clouds that produce thunderstorms and heavy rain.
• Pyrocumulonimbus clouds are a type of cumulonimbus generated by the intense heat of large wildfires.
• The fire’s heat propels smoke and air upward, where atmospheric moisture condenses into cloud.
• Lightning from these clouds can ignite new fires far from the original blaze.
• They can also inject smoke into the stratosphere, where it may linger for months.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce pyrocumulonimbus clouds to a new audience. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Pyrocumulonimbus clouds, towering thunderstorm clouds generated by the intense heat of large wildfires, can produce lightning that ignites new fires far from the original blaze.
Lightning from pyrocumulonimbus clouds can ignite new fires far from the original blaze.
When the intense heat of a large wildfire propels smoke and air upward, atmospheric moisture can condense into the kind of towering clouds that produce thunderstorms.
Pyrocumulonimbus clouds can inject smoke into the stratosphere, where it may linger for months.
items.explanation: A new audience needs to learn what pyrocumulonimbus clouds are before hearing what they do. Choice A explains that they are towering thunderstorm clouds “generated by the intense heat of large wildfires” and then gives one of their effects, lightning that can “ignite new fires far from the original blaze.”

B.recipe: AUD (uses the term without explaining it)
B.why_wrong: It gives an effect of the clouds but never says what pyrocumulonimbus clouds are.

C.why_wrong: It describes how the clouds form but never names them, so it does not introduce pyrocumulonimbus clouds.

D.recipe: AUD (uses the term without explaining it)
D.why_wrong: It gives another effect of the clouds but never says what they are or how wildfires create them.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (meteorology). Standard facts stated without a search (pyroCb clouds form over large wildfires, their lightning starts new fires, they can lift smoke into the stratosphere); no researcher or event named.

items.subtype: Emphasize how long (age filter among dated facts)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Gion Matsuri is a festival held in Kyoto, Japan, throughout the month of July.
• Its origins date back to 869, when a purification ritual was performed to halt an epidemic.
• Its highlight is a procession of more than thirty enormous wooden floats, some weighing several tons, through the city’s streets.
• Because several floats display antique tapestries, they are nicknamed “moving museums.”
• In 2009, UNESCO recognized the procession as part of the world’s intangible cultural heritage.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how long the Gion Matsuri has been held. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Every July, Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri features a procession of more than thirty enormous wooden floats through the streets of the city.
Kyoto’s Gion Matsuri has a history stretching back more than eleven centuries, to a purification ritual performed in 869.
Displaying antique tapestries, several of the Gion Matsuri’s floats are nicknamed “moving museums.”
In 2009, UNESCO recognized the Gion Matsuri’s float procession as intangible cultural heritage.
items.explanation: To emphasize how long the festival has been held, the sentence should stress its age. Choice B notes that its “origins date back to 869” and stresses that its history therefore stretches back more than eleven centuries.

A.why_wrong: It describes what the festival features each July but not how long it has been held.

C.recipe: OG (age of the decorations, not of the festival)
C.why_wrong: It mentions antique tapestries on the floats, but their age says nothing about how long the festival itself has been held.

D.why_wrong: It gives the year the procession was recognized by UNESCO, not how long the festival has existed.

items.notes: Subject: history and culture (Japanese festival). Facts known without a search (origin in 869 as a rite against an epidemic, July festival, more than thirty yamaboko floats, antique tapestries and the “moving museums” nickname, UNESCO listing in 2009). Derived phrase in the key: more than eleven centuries.

items.subtype: Explain how (orientation and its effect)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Magnetic termites inhabit the grasslands of northern Australia.
• They construct tall, narrow mounds shaped like flattened wedges.
• Each mound’s long, thin edge is aligned north to south, so its broad sides face east and west.
• The broad sides therefore receive sunlight mainly in the cooler early morning and late afternoon.
• At midday, when temperatures peak, the sun strikes only the mound’s narrow upper edge, limiting the heat it absorbs.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how the orientation of magnetic termite mounds helps keep them from overheating. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Magnetic termites in the grasslands of northern Australia construct tall, narrow mounds whose long edges are aligned north to south.
The way magnetic termites align their mounds helps limit how much heat the mounds absorb in the grasslands of northern Australia.
With its broad sides facing east and west, each magnetic termite mound catches sunlight mainly in the cooler hours, while at midday the sun strikes only its narrow upper edge.
Magnetic termite mounds are tall and narrow, shaped like flattened wedges.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how the mounds’ orientation keeps them from overheating. Choice C links the orientation, broad sides facing “east and west,” to its effect: the broad sides get sun mainly in “the cooler early morning and late afternoon,” while at midday the sun “strikes only the mound’s narrow upper edge.”

A.why_wrong: It states how the mounds are aligned but does not explain how that alignment keeps them from overheating.

B.recipe: VAGUE (asserts the effect without explaining it)
B.why_wrong: It says the alignment limits the heat the mounds absorb but never says how.

D.why_wrong: It describes the mounds’ shape but says nothing about their orientation or heat.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal architecture). Well-known natural history stated without a search (Amitermes meridionalis in northern Australia builds wedge-shaped mounds aligned north to south, broad faces catch morning and evening sun, the narrow edge faces the midday sun); no researcher named. Distinct from the live termite subjects (Odontotermes mound ventilation, Caatinga mound fields, Neocapritermes).

review.notes: Soft overlap judged acceptable: live termite items are Caatinga mound fields (boundaries w2), Namib fairy circles (RS b7) and zai pits (RS); the Odontotermes ventilation claim was withdrawn. Mound orientation of the magnetic termite is a distinct subject.

items.subtype: Explain an advantage (one thing over another)
items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Seawalls are concrete or stone barriers built along coastlines to prevent erosion.
• Waves striking a seawall rebound, which can wash away sand at the wall’s base.
• Living shorelines instead use natural features, such as marsh vegetation and oyster reefs, to protect the coast.
• These features absorb the energy of incoming waves rather than reflecting it.
• Cordgrasses are among the marsh plants commonly used in living shorelines.
items.stem: The student wants to explain an advantage of living shorelines over seawalls. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Unlike seawalls, which reflect waves in a way that can wash away sand at their base, living shorelines absorb the energy of incoming waves.
Living shorelines rely on natural features, such as oyster reefs and marsh vegetation like cordgrasses, to protect coastlines from erosion.
Seawalls are concrete or stone barriers that reflect incoming waves, which can wash away sand at their base.
Living shorelines and seawalls both protect coastlines from erosion, but they do so in strikingly different ways.
items.explanation: An advantage of living shorelines over seawalls must show what the first does better than the second. Choice A does: waves striking a seawall “rebound, which can wash away sand at the wall’s base,” whereas living shorelines “absorb the energy of incoming waves rather than reflecting it.”

B.why_wrong: It says what living shorelines are made of but never compares them with seawalls or gives an advantage.

C.why_wrong: It gives a drawback of seawalls but never mentions living shorelines.

items.notes: Subject: history and culture (games).
